But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.<sup>27</sup>And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment,<sup>28</sup>so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

10.title: Once for All: The New and Living Way
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the summit of the letter’s central argument. Priesthood (chapters 5–7), covenant (8) and sacrifice (9) converge here. The law’s yearly animal sacrifices are set against Christ’s single offering, with Psalm 40 as the key: “I have come to do your will, O God.” By that will, through the offering of his body once for all, “we have been sanctified.”

Then the longest application (vv. 19–39): draw near to God, hold fast the confession, and stir one another up to love and good works. The fourth and severest warning follows (vv. 26–31), balanced at once by encouragement: remember how you once joyfully accepted the loss of your property. You need endurance for a little while more. The coming one will come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — One Sacrifice, and a Priest Who Sat Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law is only a shadow and can never make worshippers perfect; otherwise the yearly sacrifices would have stopped. Instead they were an annual reminder of sins, since animal blood cannot take sins away. So Christ, coming into the world, said: “You did not desire sacrifices, but a body you prepared for me. I have come to do your will.” By that will we have been made holy through the offering of his body once for all. Every priest stands daily; Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down. By one offering he has perfected for all time those who are being made holy. And where sins are forgiven, no further offering is needed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Tenses in One Sentence

By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Where sins are forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins, and their repetition confessed that they had not finished the work.

Now: Standing before God does not wait on our progress; our progress flows from a finished offering.

verseByVerse.quote: For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves. So it can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have stopped being offered? The worshippers would have been cleansed once for all and no longer feel guilty for their sins.

Shadow and form. “True form” is eikōn, the actual likeness. A shadow tells you a body is there and roughly its shape. You cannot shake hands with it.

Never. Not a system that worked imperfectly, but one that could not finish the job.

Repetition as evidence. If the Day of Atonement had settled the matter, there would be no need for another next autumn. The calendar coming round again confessed that nothing was concluded.

The test. A sacrifice that truly worked would leave no nagging guilt, not because of hardness, but because the matter was settled.

On a Tuesday. If you are trying to quiet the same accusation this year as last, with more effort and more religious activity, the method is not working. Look to the one sacrifice that does.

verseByVerse.quote: But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

A reminder. The Day of Atonement is thought of as the day sins were dealt with. Its actual effect was to bring them to mind. The high priest confessed the nation’s sins over the goat (Leviticus 16:21): an annual reading of the books aloud.

Impossible. Not inadequate, but impossible. Sin is a moral matter between a person and God. An animal is neither a person nor a moral agent; it has consented to nothing.

What were they for? A language taught for fourteen centuries: sin costs life, God provides the victim, the innocent dies for the guilty. So that when the reality came, there would be words to describe it.

Were Old Testament believers forgiven? Yes, truly, but not by the animals. They were forgiven by grace through faith, on the credit of Christ’s coming sacrifice (9:15; Romans 3:25). The sacrifices were the means their faith used to lay hold of God’s promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when Christ came into the world, he said: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me; with burnt offerings and sin offerings you were not pleased. Then I said, ‘Here I am; it is written about me in the scroll; I have come to do your will, my God.’”

The Son speaks Psalm 40. The writer hears the psalm as the Son’s words to the Father at his incarnation.

Not desired? God commanded sacrifices; he is not renouncing them. The prophets use the same comparative idiom: “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). Not these, but what they pointed to.

A body. The Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 reads “ears you have dug for me”, probably ears opened to hear and obey. The Greek Old Testament reads “a body you have prepared for me”. They agree: God wanted not an animal but a life at his disposal. God did not want a body brought to the altar; he prepared one, and it walked there.

I have come. No bargaining, no conditions. Just arrival and willingness.

Written of me. The incarnation was not an improvised rescue. It was in the book.
verseByVerse.note: “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew of Ps 40:6 reads “you have given me an open ear.”

verseByVerse.quote: When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First he said, “Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings you did not desire, nor were you pleased with them”, though the law required them. Then he said, “Here I am, I have come to do your will.” He sets aside the first to establish the second. And by that will, we have been made holy through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

Reading the order. First a negative, then a positive. The second replaces the first. The Son takes one down and sets the other up.

By that will. God’s will, which the Son came to do. Not our willing, but his.

Have been sanctified. A Greek perfect: completed, with the result standing. It has happened.

Two senses. Verse 14 will speak of those “being sanctified”. Both are true, and the order matters: set apart definitively by what Christ did, then progressively made to match it. The second is a lifetime’s work. The first is finished.

verseByVerse.quote: And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day after day every priest stands and performs his religious duties; again and again he offers the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, and since then he waits for his enemies to be made his footstool. For by one sacrifice he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy.

Stands. There were no chairs in the tabernacle. Exodus lists the furniture, and no seat appears.

He sat down. The finality of the cross, told by a posture: a man sitting down in a building without chairs.

Waiting. Atonement is finished; the subduing of enemies is not (Psalm 110:1). That is why the readers suffered.

Two tenses. Perfected for all time: done. Being sanctified: still in progress this morning. In God’s sight, on the basis of one offering, they are finished; in experience, halfway and struggling.

Get them in the right order. If you think your standing depends on your progress, you will never rest. If you think progress does not matter, you have not understood what you were set apart for.

On a Tuesday. When you fail again, say: “I am still being sanctified, and I have been perfected for all time by his one offering.” Then get up and keep going.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First he says, “This is the covenant I will make with them after that time, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts and write them on their minds.” Then he adds, “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” And where these have been forgiven, sacrifice for sin is no longer necessary.

The Spirit testifies now. Present tense, as at 3:7.

Two clauses chosen. The law on the heart, and sins remembered no more. The purpose arrives in v. 18.

The inference. If God will never bring sins up again, there is nothing left for a sacrifice to do. Where the matter is closed, an offering is not just unnecessary but unintelligible. Going back to the temple would be to keep offering for sins God has promised not to remember, which implies the promise is false.

No repeatable offering. The New Testament knows sacrifices of praise and doing good (13:15–16), and our bodies as living sacrifices (Romans 12:1). It knows no repeatable offering for sin, and this verse is why. Whatever the church does when it gathers, including the Lord’s Supper, it is not offering a sacrifice for sin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–39 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Therefore, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by Jesus’ blood, by the new and living way through the curtain, his flesh, and since we have a great priest over God’s house: let us draw near with a sincere heart, cleansed; let us hold fast our hope, because he who promised is faithful; and let us think how to spur one another on to love and good deeds, not giving up meeting together. If we deliberately keep on sinning after knowing the truth, no sacrifice remains, only judgment. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. But remember your earlier courage, when you joyfully accepted the loss of property. Do not throw away your confidence; you need endurance. The coming one will come. We are not those who shrink back, but those who believe and are saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtain Is His Flesh

The way into the holy places has been opened through the curtain, his flesh. So draw near, hold fast because he who promised is faithful, and stir one another up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had once joyfully accepted the plundering of their property.

Now: The warning of verses 26–31 is aimed at deliberate repudiation of Christ, not at a struggling believer; and it ends in assurance: we are not of those who shrink back.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way opened for us through the curtain, that is, his body, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,

Therefore. Nine chapters of argument now become three commands.

Confidence. Parrēsia, as at 4:16. The room one man entered once a year is open.

By the blood. The only ground. Not sincerity or improvement.

New and living. Fresh, and alive, because the way is a person.

The curtain is his flesh. The barrier was opened by its tearing. When Jesus died, the temple veil was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), from above. His body was torn, and the barrier with it.

A beautiful barrier. The curtain was blue, purple and scarlet, worked with cherubim. The barrier between God and us was magnificent, and it had to be destroyed.

A great priest. Not only an open way, but a man at the end of it who belongs to us.

verseByVerse.quote: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
let us draw near to God with a sincere heart and with the full assurance that faith brings, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.

Draw near. The priestly verb, now commanded of everyone.

True heart. Genuine, without pretence or borrowed words.

Full assurance. Not certainty about ourselves, but about the ground: the blood, the way, the priest.

Done to us. Both remaining verbs are passive. Hearts sprinkled, as priests were at ordination (Exodus 29:21), cleansing the conscience the old sacrifices could not reach (9:9). Bodies washed, as priests were (Exodus 29:4), and as God promised: “I will sprinkle clean water on you” (Ezekiel 36:25).

Baptism? Some read the washing as purely figurative. The more likely reading is that the writer means baptism, as the outward sign of the inward cleansing named in the same breath. Even so, the water does not cleanse; Christ’s blood does. Baptism is the sign of it, given to those who have drawn near in faith (1 Peter 3:21).

What is missing. No requirement of worthiness, no waiting period, no measure of progress. A throne you must qualify for is not a throne of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us hold unswervingly to the hope we profess, for he who promised is faithful.

The confession. What they said publicly, probably at baptism, and what got their property seized.

Without wavering. Not tilting between two positions.

His faithfulness. Not “hold on because you are strong”, but because he is faithful. A man gritting his teeth relies on his grip, and grips fail. A man holding fast because the promiser is faithful relies on something outside himself.

Hope. About something not yet in hand, which is why holding it takes anything at all.

The answer to drift. A drifting church is not usually losing an argument but its grip in the dark. The writer points to God’s character and says: hold on to that.

On a Tuesday. When doubt whispers, do not first examine your feelings. Name one promise God has made, and say aloud, “He who promised is faithful.”

verseByVerse.quote: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And let us consider how we may spur one another on towards love and good deeds, not giving up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

Consider. The verb of 3:1, used of Jesus. Working out how to help a particular person forward needs the same attention as contemplating Christ.

Stir up. Paroxysmos, from which “paroxysm” comes: a sharp provocation, the word for Paul and Barnabas’s quarrel (Acts 15:39). Provoke one another, but to love and good works. The friend who will not let you settle.

A habit of absence. The first concrete symptom: some had stopped coming. Not a decision, a pattern. The reasons may have been good: meeting was dangerous. The writer names it anyway, because you cannot stir or be stirred from a distance.

Online church? The word is about gathering in one place, and stirring up needs people present to each other. For the sick, the housebound and the persecuted, a livestream is a real mercy, and no one should feel guilty for what they cannot help. But for those who can come, watching is not meeting, and a settled habit of staying away is the drift this verse warns against.

All the more. Under pressure, the instinct is to withdraw. The nearer the Day, the more of this, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we deliberately keep on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is left, only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume God’s enemies.

Deliberately. First in the Greek sentence. A technical term: the law distinguished unintentional sins, for which sacrifice was provided (Leviticus 4), from sin “with a high hand”, for which there was none (Numbers 15:30–31).

Go on. Persisting: a settled course, not a fall.

With knowledge. Not the sin of the ignorant or deceived.

The sin in view. The informed, deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ (v. 29: trampling the Son of God underfoot).

No sacrifice remains. There is one sacrifice. Rejecting it is not exhausting a supply but refusing the only one there is.

What it does not mean. These verses have terrified people they were never aimed at. They do not describe a Christian who has sinned badly or repeatedly, or who is fighting a besetting sin and losing. Such a person has a sacrifice, and the whole letter urges him to come and use it. This describes someone who has looked at the sacrifice and trampled on it.

Adversaries. Isaiah’s language (Isaiah 26:11). This awaits enemies, not stumbling sons.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much more severely do you think someone deserves to be punished who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, treated as unholy the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace? We know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay”, and again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a terrifying thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

Lesser to greater. Deuteronomy 17:6: idolatry was punished by death on witnesses’ testimony.

Three descriptions. Trampled the Son underfoot. Treated the covenant blood as common. Insulted the Spirit of grace.

“By which he was sanctified”. Most likely set apart in the outward sense, as a member of the covenant community, as Israel was sanctified at Sinai. Like the field that drank the same rain (6:7–8).

Can a true believer fall into this? Arminians say yes, pointing to “was sanctified”. Some take the warning as hypothetical. Others hold it describes someone who belonged to the community, knew the truth and shared its privileges, but never truly trusted Christ, and finally walked away (6:4–8). The last is more likely, and the letter points that way: “we are not of those who shrink back” (v. 39), and Christ saves to the uttermost (7:25). God keeps his own, and warnings like this are among his means.

His people. Not the nations: the Lord will judge his people, words Moses first sang over Israel (Deuteronomy 32:36). Belonging to the community is no shelter; judgment begins there (1 Peter 4:17).

The hands of the living God. To fall away is to fall from the living God (3:12), and there is nowhere to fall but into his hands. The same hands are the only refuge and the only danger.

For worship. Let this verse make you tremble, and then run to the same hands for mercy. That is the fear of the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember those earlier days after you had received the light, when you endured a hard struggle with suffering. Sometimes you were publicly exposed to insult and persecution; at other times you stood side by side with those who were so treated. You suffered along with those in prison, and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, because you knew that you had better and lasting possessions.

The tone changes. Having brought them to the edge, he reminds them who they are.

After the light. Becoming Christians is what brought the suffering.

A spectacle. A theatre word: put on stage, publicly shamed, in a culture where honour was everything.

Partners. It takes its own courage to walk over and stand beside someone who has been dragged out.

Prisoners. Visiting meant identifying with the accused, and prisoners depended on visitors for food. They went.

Joyfully. Not endured, not tolerated. Joyfully accepted their houses being emptied, with no legal recourse.

How. Not stoicism, but knowing they owned something no mob could reach.

Be what you were. He is not asking them to become something new, but to be what they already were.

On a Tuesday. Remember the early days of your faith, the courage and joy you had. That was not naivety. It was true, and it still is.
verseByVerse.note: Possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not throw away your confidence; it will be richly rewarded. You need to persevere, so that when you have done the will of God, you will receive what he has promised.

Throw away. Not “lose”, as if it slipped out of a pocket, but discard on purpose, like a soldier throwing away his shield to run faster.

Confidence. Parrēsia: access, boldness. There is a quietness that looks like humility and is really the shield going over the wall.

A great reward. The writer is not embarrassed by the motive (11:6, 26).

Need of endurance. After ten chapters of theology, the diagnosis: not better arguments, but staying power. People do not usually leave the faith because they have run out of reasons.

Do, then receive. Not earned, but at the end of a road that must actually be walked. Endurance is not waiting; it is continuing to obey while nothing visible changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, “In just a little while, he who is coming will come and will not delay.” And, “My righteous one will live by faith. And I take no pleasure in the one who shrinks back.”

Habakkuk. The prophet of waiting: “How long, O LORD?” The answer: “If it seems slow, wait for it” (Habakkuk 2:3).

A little while, how little. The Greek doubles the word to press its shortness. And where the Hebrew speaks of a vision coming, the Greek Old Testament speaks of a person: “the coming one”.

Live by faith. Paul uses this to answer how a sinner is justified (Romans 1:17). Hebrews uses it to answer how a believer keeps going. The emphasis falls on live: not only beginning by faith, but living by it daily. Chapter 11 illustrates it.

Shrinks back. To draw back from danger. Faith goes forward when it cannot see; shrinking back is faith failing, like Israel at the border.

No pleasure. Not rage, but the withdrawal of delight, which from God is worse.

verseByVerse.quote: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we do not belong to those who shrink back and are destroyed, but to those who have faith and are saved.

We. He includes himself and his readers, firmly on the right side.

A category, not an achievement. Not “we performed better”, but “we belong to a different kind”.

The pattern. As at 6:9, the strongest warning is followed by assurance. Warning and assurance are not alternatives. The warning is one of the means by which the assurance proves true.

Defined by faith. Not endurance or works, though both are commanded. Faith distinguishes those who arrive from those who turn back.

The next chapter. Having said faith is the difference, the writer defines it, then produces a crowd of people who had it.

For worship. If you trust Christ, this verse is about you. Thank God that you are not among those who shrink back, and ask him to keep you.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near.<sup>2</sup>Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?<sup>3</sup>But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.<sup>5</sup>Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me;<sup>6</sup>in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure.<sup>7</sup>Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”<sup>8</sup>When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law),<sup>9</sup>then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.<sup>10</sup>And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.<sup>11</sup>And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.<sup>12</sup>But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God,<sup>13</sup>waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet.<sup>14</sup>For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.<sup>15</sup>And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying,<sup>16</sup>“This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,”<sup>17</sup>then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.”<sup>18</sup>Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.<sup>19</sup>Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus,<sup>20</sup>by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh,<sup>21</sup>and since we have a great priest over the house of God,<sup>22</sup>let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.<sup>23</sup>Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.<sup>24</sup>And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works,<sup>25</sup>not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.<sup>26</sup>For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,<sup>27</sup>but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.<sup>28</sup>Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>29</sup>How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?<sup>30</sup>For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.”<sup>31</sup>It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.<sup>32</sup>But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,<sup>33</sup>sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated.<sup>34</sup>For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.<sup>35</sup>Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.<sup>36</sup>For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.<sup>37</sup>For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay;<sup>38</sup>but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”<sup>39</sup>But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

11.title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
11.overview:
Ten chapters have argued that Jesus is better. Chapter 11 shows what it looks like to live on that: a gallery of people who took God at his word about things they could not see, and acted on it. Faith here is never an opinion held; it is always something done that makes no sense without a promise from God.

The gallery is honest. Its members are often inconsistent (Sarah laughed, Jacob deceived, Samson was a disgrace), and its outcomes are opposite: some shut lions’ mouths, some were sawn in two. All are commended, and none received what was promised. The chapter ends by saying why: God was keeping something better, so that they and we would be made perfect together. The readers were tempted to go back to the age these saints longed to see the end of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — By Faith: Title Deeds and Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith gives a present footing to what is hoped for and proves what is unseen; by it the saints of old were approved. By faith we know God made the world by his word. Abel offered a better sacrifice; Enoch pleased God and did not die; without faith no one can please God. Noah built the ark. Abraham left home not knowing where he was going, and lived in tents in the promised land, looking for God’s city. Sarah conceived past the age. All these died without receiving the promises, confessing they were strangers seeking a heavenly country, and God is not ashamed to be their God. Abraham offered Isaac, reckoning God could raise him; Isaac, Jacob and Joseph blessed and gave directions in faith as they died.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as a Title Deed

Faith gives the things hoped for a footing in the present, because it rests on the reliability of the one who promised. Everyone in this gallery is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in tents in the land of promise and died without receiving it.

Now: God is not ashamed to be called the God of people who are visibly waiting for a better country.

verseByVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith is being sure of what we hope for and convinced of what we cannot see. It is what the people of old were commended for.

Assurance. Hypostasis, “that which stands under”. In the papyri it can mean a title deed: the document that gives you a claim now to property you do not yet hold. Faith gives the future a footing in the present.

Conviction. Elenchos, a law-court word: proof that settles a case.

What it does not mean. Not a leap in the dark, and not believing harder than the evidence allows. The ground of faith is not the strength of the believing but the reliability of the one who promised (10:23). It is not a definition of every aspect of faith either, but a description of what faith does.

Commended. Literally “witnessed to”. God himself is the witness, and the word recurs (vv. 4, 5, 39).

On a Tuesday. You make decisions daily on testimony: the doctor’s diagnosis, the bank’s statement, the timetable. Faith is doing that with the most reliable testimony there is.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith we understand that God made the universe by speaking, so that the visible world did not come from anything visible.

Faith and understanding. Not opposites. Faith is how this is known; nobody watched creation happen, so everyone who believes it does so on testimony.

By the word. As Genesis says: God spoke, and it was. Not shaped from earlier material: out of nothing.

How long? This verse does not say. Many Christians read Genesis 1 as long ages, or as a literary framework, to fit an old earth. The plainest reading, confirmed by the fourth commandment, is six ordinary days: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth (Exod 20:11). That is the view taken here, held with respect for those who differ.

Why start here? The chapter is about acting on what cannot be seen. If the visible came from the invisible, the invisible is the more solid of the two. Moses will act on that (v. 27).

For worship. The God who spoke galaxies into being has spoken to you. His word is not weaker on Tuesday than it was on the first day.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abel’s sacrifice was accepted because he offered it in faith, and though he was murdered his faith still speaks. Enoch pleased God, and God took him without his dying.

Why Abel’s? Genesis does not say; Hebrews does: faith. Some think the difference was blood against grain. But the text puts it in the worshipper, not the offering: “The LORD had regard for Abel and his offering” (Genesis 4:4), the man first. The same act done by two people is not the same act.

Still speaks. In Genesis his blood cries from the ground (4:10); here his faith goes on talking. Everyone in this chapter is dead, and every one is still speaking.

Enoch. In a chapter of Genesis that ends each life with “and he died”, one man has no death recorded (5:24). “Walked with God” appears in the Greek Old Testament as “pleased God”, which leads to verse 6.

Opposite outcomes. Abel died young and violently; Enoch did not die. Both are commended. Faith is not a guarantee of how things go.

verseByVerse.quote: And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without faith no one can please God, because anyone who comes to him must believe that he is there and that he rewards those who seek him.

Impossible. The letter’s strongest word (6:4, 18; 10:4). Decent living without faith does not please God less; it does not please him at all (Romans 14:23). To do good without trusting him is to treat him as someone to be managed rather than believed.

Two modest beliefs. That he exists, and that seeking him is not knocking at an empty house. The second is harder. Many believe in God and expect nothing from praying.

Rewards. Not mercenary, because the reward is God himself.

Those who have never heard? Some Christians hold that God may save people who respond sincerely to what light they have, or will give a chance after death. But this verse does not say vague belief is enough. The faith that pleases God draws near through Christ (7:25); this letter closes the door on a second chance (9:27); and salvation comes by hearing (Romans 10:14). God sent Peter to the seeking Cornelius (Acts 10). The answer is not to speculate about them but to go to them.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Warned by God about something no one had seen, Noah took him seriously and built the ark to save his family. In doing so he showed up the unbelief of the world and inherited the righteousness that comes by faith.

Reverent fear. Godly caution, the word used of Christ at 5:7. Noah took God at his word.

Faith visible. A very large wooden boat, built over many years, in full view of neighbours. No one in this chapter is commended for holding an opinion; each did something that only made sense if God had spoken.

Condemned the world. Not by scolding it, though Peter calls him a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5), but by acting as if God’s word were true. Obedience is a verdict on those who heard the same word and did nothing.

Heir of righteousness by faith. Paul’s phrase, on a man before Abraham and before the law. It has always worked this way.

A real flood. Hebrews, Peter and Jesus (Matthew 24:37–39) treat it as history and as a pattern of the coming judgment. Some Christians take it as a regional flood; the language of Genesis 7:19–23 points to a universal one.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God called Abraham, he obeyed and set out without knowing where he was going. In the promised land he lived as a foreigner, in tents, with Isaac and Jacob, because he was waiting for the city with foundations that God designs and builds.

Obey, then find out. God said go, and told him where after he went (Genesis 12:1). Security then was land and kin, and he left both at seventy-five.

A stranger at home. He arrived and was still a foreigner. The only ground he ever owned was a grave (Genesis 23).

Tents and foundations. A tent is the least permanent home there is; foundations are the part of a building that does not move. Abraham could live in the temporary because he expected the permanent.

What it does not mean. Not that faith despises earthly things or refuses to plan. Abraham kept flocks and bought a field. It means holding them loosely, as a guest.

On a Tuesday. The house, the pension, the career: live in them as tents. The readers had lost their property (10:34). They were not losing a city.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Sarah received the power to conceive when she was too old, because she judged that God, who had promised, was faithful. So from one man, as good as dead, came descendants as many as the stars and the sand.

A generous commendation. Sarah laughed at the promise and then denied it (Genesis 18:12–15); she had arranged Hagar rather than wait. God commends the faith that was really there under a mixed performance.

Faithful who had promised. Faith is a judgement about the character of God, not a feeling about the odds.

As good as dead. Paul says it too (Romans 4:19). The situation was not unlikely; it was closed.

Whose faith? A textual and grammatical puzzle. The phrase “power to conceive” is literally “power for the laying down of seed”, normally said of the father, and some manuscripts add that Sarah was barren. So some translations make Abraham the subject: “By faith Abraham, with Sarah, received power to become a father.” The ESV keeps Sarah as subject. Either reading is possible; Sarah is the more natural subject of the sentence as it stands, and both readings commend the same trust.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All of them died trusting God without receiving what was promised. They saw it from far off and welcomed it, and said they were strangers on earth. That shows they were looking for a homeland: not the one they left, or they could have gone back, but a better, heavenly one. So God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

Died without receiving. Without the land, the nation or the promised offspring. But not without salvation: they were saved by faith in the Christ who was to come, and his death covers their sins too (9:15).

Greeted from afar. Like travellers waving at a coastline they will not reach on this voyage.

Strangers. Abraham’s own words: “I am a sojourner and foreigner among you” (Genesis 23:4). Whoever calls himself a stranger has said he belongs elsewhere.

No return ticket. Ur was still there. Their homesickness was not for anywhere they had left.

Not ashamed. God calls himself the God of three men who lived in tents and died owning a grave. People visibly waiting for his country do not embarrass him. It is those settled here who make the title awkward.

For worship. He has prepared a city. The hope is not a wish. It is built.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God tested Abraham, he offered up Isaac, his only son, although God had said that his line would come through Isaac. He reasoned that God could raise Isaac from the dead, and in a figure he did receive him back.

The test. Isaac was the promise in a body. Abraham was asked to obey a command that seemed to destroy the promise it came from: to trust God against God.

How could God command it? He never meant it to be done. It was a test, and he stopped Abraham’s hand (Genesis 22:1, 12). The same God forbids child sacrifice in the plainest terms (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). The story gives no one warrant to harm anyone in God’s name.

Considered. A reckoning word. Not blind obedience but reasoning: the promise runs through Isaac; God cannot lie; so God will raise him. No one had ever been raised, and Abraham inferred resurrection from God’s character alone. Hence his words to the servants: “I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you” (Genesis 22:5).

Figuratively. En parabolē, “in a parable”. A father, an only son, wood carried up a hill, a substitute provided by God. Two thousand years later God did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32).

On a Tuesday. When God’s providence seems to contradict his promise, reason as Abraham did: from who God is, not from what you can see.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac, Jacob and Joseph each showed faith as they were dying. Isaac blessed his sons about the future. Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons and worshipped, leaning on his staff. Joseph spoke of the coming exodus and told them to carry his bones out of Egypt.

Dying men, a future unseen. All three acts look past their own lives.

Isaac. Blind, deceived, intending the blessing for Esau. When he found out, he trembled and said of Jacob, “yes, and he shall be blessed” (Genesis 27:33). He bowed to God’s purpose running through his own mistake.

Jacob. He crossed his hands to bless the younger (Genesis 48:14). The man who stole a blessing ends by giving them away.

Staff or bed? Hebrews follows the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 47:31, “staff”; the Hebrew reads “bed”. The consonants of the two Hebrew words are identical, and only the vowels, added much later, differ. Either is a true picture of a weak old man worshipping, and the writer is free to quote the Bible his readers used.

Joseph. Second man in Egypt, settled in the best land. And he made them swear to carry his coffin out. For centuries his bones sat in Egypt as a statement that this was not home. Moses took them (Exodus 13:19); they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32).

On a Tuesday. How you plan your death, will and funeral can be a confession of faith. Joseph’s was.
verseByVerse.note: “Staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Gen 47:31; the Hebrew text as later pointed reads “bed”; the consonants are the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–40 — The Turn: Some Were Tortured
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses’ parents hid him, unafraid of Pharaoh. Grown, Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing ill-treatment with God’s people over sin’s brief pleasures, and counting the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. He left Egypt unafraid, as seeing the invisible God, and kept the Passover. Israel crossed the Red Sea; Jericho’s walls fell; Rahab was spared. There is no time to tell of the judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, who won battles and escaped death. Then the turn: others were tortured, mocked, stoned, sawn in two, homeless, people the world was not worthy of. All were commended, and none received the promise, because God planned something better, so that they would be made perfect only with us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Chapter Turns Over Mid-Verse

In verse 35 faith that raised the dead becomes faith that was tortured to death — the same faith, opposite outcomes, both commended. Of such people the world was not worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel were far from consistent, and they are in the roll.

Now: All these died waiting for what the church now has; apart from us they are not made perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ parents hid him for three months, unafraid of Pharaoh’s order. When he grew up, Moses refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose to be ill-treated with God’s people rather than enjoy sin for a short time, because he counted disgrace for Christ worth more than Egypt’s treasures. He was looking to the reward.

His parents first. The first act of faith belongs to a mother and father with a baby in a basket, who, like the midwives, feared God rather than the king (Exodus 1:17).

What he refused. The royal household of the greatest power on earth, its learning and its wealth (Acts 7:22).

Fleeting. The pleasures of sin are real. Hebrews does not pretend Egypt was miserable. But they last a season. Moses’ choice was not asceticism but arithmetic about time.

The reproach of Christ. Moses lived fourteen centuries before Jesus. Some take it to mean the reproach Moses bore for God’s anointed people. More likely the writer means it plainly: the Messiah was already identified with his people, so their disgrace was his (compare 1 Corinthians 10:4), and Moses chose to share it.

Greater wealth. A commercial word. He did not weigh spiritual benefit against material loss; he weighed one wealth against another.

On a Tuesday. Being the one at work who will not join in has a cost. Count it honestly, and count the reward too.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Moses left Egypt without fear of the king’s anger, holding on because he saw the God no one can see. By faith he kept the Passover and put the blood on the doorposts, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel.

Not afraid? Exodus says Moses fled to Midian because he was afraid (Exodus 2:14). Most likely Hebrews means the exodus itself, since the Passover follows. Others think it means the flight, read as a refusal to bow rather than panic. Either way Hebrews is not rewriting history.

Seeing the invisible. The paradox is deliberate. Moses stood before the most visible power on earth unimpressed, because he was looking at someone else in the room.

Endured. The word of 10:36: staying under the weight. The seeing produced forty years of staying put.

The blood. Nothing about blood on a doorframe looks protective. Israelites were not spared for being Israelites, but because the blood was there. The whole letter in one night.

For worship. Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). Judgment passes over every house under his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Israel crossed the Red Sea on dry ground, while the Egyptians who tried it drowned. By faith Jericho’s walls fell after seven days of marching. By faith Rahab, the prostitute, was not destroyed with the disobedient, because she welcomed the spies.

Same seabed. Egypt did exactly what Israel did and drowned. The difference was not the action but what stood behind it.

Seven days. An army walking in silence round a city, watched from the walls. Nothing happened for six days. Faith often looks foolish for a while before it looks like anything.

Rahab the prostitute. The writer keeps the word, and puts a Canaanite woman of that trade straight after Moses. She heard of the Red Sea and believed more on less evidence than anyone in Jericho (Joshua 2:9–11). She ended in the line of Christ (Matthew 1:5).

Her lie. She lied to the king’s men (Joshua 2:4–5). Some Christians hold that deceiving would-be murderers is not the false witness the commandment forbids, and point to the midwives, with whom “God dealt well” (Exodus 1:20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that the lie was a sin, forgiven with the rest of her past. The second is more likely: Scripture commends her faith and her welcome (James 2:25), never the lie. God honoured her trust in spite of it, which should comfort anyone whose faith has been mixed with sin.

On a Tuesday. No past puts you outside this family. It always had a Canaanite prostitute in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no time to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets, who by faith won kingdoms, ruled justly, received what God promised, shut lions’ mouths, put out fire, escaped the sword, were made strong when weak, and routed armies.

Time would fail. A preacher’s skill: the sense of an endless supply says more than twenty more examples.

Unlikely names. Gideon wanted signs. Barak would not go without Deborah. Samson was ruled by appetite. Jephthah made a rash vow. David committed adultery and murder. Samuel’s sons took bribes. The roll does not measure character. It measures having taken God at his word, in lives that were often a mess.

What it does not mean. Not that their sins did not matter, or that Jephthah’s vow is approved. Judges tells those stories as warnings. Faith is commended; folly is not.

Obtained promises. Not a contradiction of v. 39. They received particular promises: victories, deliverances. Not the great promise, Christ and his city.

Strong out of weakness. Passive: made strong. The strength came from elsewhere.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges; the lions’ mouths recall Daniel, and the fire recalls his three friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women received their dead raised to life. Others were tortured and would not accept release, so that they might rise to a better resurrection. Others were mocked, flogged, chained and imprisoned. They were stoned, sawn in two, killed with the sword. They wandered in animal skins, poor, oppressed and ill-treated, living in deserts, mountains and caves. The world was not worthy of them.

The turn. Mid-verse, faith that got the dead back becomes faith that was tortured to death. Same faith, opposite outcomes, both commended.

Who is meant? The widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite received their sons back (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4). Those who refused release probably include the martyrs under Antiochus told of in 2 Maccabees 6–7. Hebrews may allude to that history without treating the book as Scripture, as Jude cites Enoch. Zechariah was stoned (2 Chronicles 24:21); tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “they were tempted” to the list in v. 37, an odd item among violent deaths. It is missing from the earliest papyrus and looks like a copying slip for a similar Greek word (“they were burned”, perhaps). The ESV rightly leaves it out.

Not worthy. The world looked at them in goatskins and thought them worthless. God says the world was not good enough for them.

On a Tuesday. Faith does not guarantee a rescue. If yours has brought no deliverance, it may have brought you into this second half of the list, of whom God is not ashamed either.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All of these were commended for their faith, yet none received what was promised, because God had planned something better that includes us, so that they would not be made perfect without us.

Still waiting. The conquerors and the martyrs alike, all commended, none satisfied.

Something better. All the letter has argued: the better covenant, sacrifice and priest. They saw from afar; we have the substance.

Together. Abraham is not completed without the church. There is one people of God, not two, saved by one faith through one sacrifice.

Where were they meanwhile? Some traditions teach that Old Testament believers waited in a place below until Christ freed them. Scripture gives little ground for it. Jesus promised the thief paradise “today” (Luke 23:43), and Hebrews speaks of “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” already in God’s presence (12:23). They are with God now. What they wait for, with us, is the resurrection of the body.

The irony. The readers were drifting back to the age these giants lived in and longed to see ended. The whole gallery died waiting for what this discouraged congregation already had.

For worship. The stands are full, and the runners are not alone (12:1).
